title: Only Happens Here: 10 Things That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
description: Antwerp turns its own mythology, dialect, printing history, fashion nerve and river engineering into everyday objects: edible hands, dressed saints, basement puppets and a beer named after its glass.

cards.title: Antwerpse Handjes
cards.subtitle: The city’s severed-hand legend became a regulated biscuit.
cards.notes: Created by pastry chef Jos Hakker for a 1934 competition, these almond-topped, hand-shaped biscuits translate the Brabo-and-Antigoon story into something edible. Their recipe, form and packaging were later protected, and production is restricted to members of Antwerp’s bakers’ union—a very Antwerp way to formalize civic folklore.
cards.short_summary: A protected hand-shaped biscuit born from Antwerp’s founding legend and bakers’ guild.

cards.title: De Poesje van Antwerpen
cards.subtitle: Adult puppet theatre survives in a cellar, in broad Antwerp dialect.
cards.notes: Poesjenellen are rod puppets descended from Italian street theatre and embedded in Antwerp popular culture since the 16th century. The surviving cellar tradition is comic, satirical and emphatically not children’s theatre: characters swear, fight and sing in plat Antwerps. Performances are booked by groups rather than through ordinary individual ticketing.
cards.short_summary: A basement rod-puppet theatre where satire is still delivered in raw Antwerp dialect.
cards.source_title: De Poesje van Antwerpen | MAS | Museum aan de Stroom

cards.title: Sint-Annatunnel
cards.subtitle: A river crossing reached by monumental wooden escalators.
cards.notes: Built in 1931–33 to join Antwerp’s two Scheldt banks, the pedestrian tunnel survives with its entrance buildings and much of its original technical equipment. Flemish heritage authorities describe it as a uniquely preserved example of an under-river pedestrian tunnel equipped with lifts and escalators. In a port city divided by a broad working river, the elaborate descent makes practical sense.
cards.short_summary: Antwerp crosses the Scheldt through a protected 1930s pedestrian tunnel and its preserved machinery.

cards.title: The Antwerp Six
cards.subtitle: A fashion movement named like a municipal delegation.
cards.notes: Dirk Bikkembergs, Ann Demeulemeester, Walter Van Beirendonck, Dries Van Noten, Dirk Van Saene and Marina Yee studied at Antwerp’s Royal Academy, then broke internationally after presenting in London in 1986. The geographic nickname stuck because their shared city and school were the connective tissue—even as they built separate labels.
cards.short_summary: Six Academy-trained designers turned their city’s name into fashion shorthand.
cards.source_title: The Antwerp Six | MoMu - Fashion Museum Antwerp

cards.title: Semini at Het Steen
cards.subtitle: A damaged fertility figure still receives an annual civic celebration.
cards.notes: Above Het Steen’s gateway sits a battered relief traditionally identified as Semini. Antwerp women once appealed to the supposed fertility god when hoping for children; how much of that story is historically true remains uncertain. A local preservation committee deliberately keeps the legend alive through walks, puppetry and an annual Grote Markt celebration.
cards.short_summary: A mysterious relief over Antwerp’s old fortress gate sustains a knowingly half-legendary fertility ritual.
cards.source_title: Antwerps Komitee Semini in Ere (AKSIE) | Antwerpen

cards.title: Ann Demeulemeester’s Madonna
cards.subtitle: A Gothic church’s Virgin wears contemporary Antwerp fashion.
cards.notes: The statue’s clothing was designed by Ann Demeulemeester, placing one of the Antwerp Six inside a historic neighborhood church. It works here because St. Andrew’s stands in the fashion district, where the parish presents old rituals through contemporary visual language rather than treating fashion and devotion as separate worlds.
cards.short_summary: An Antwerp Six designer dressed the Virgin Mary in a church inside the city’s fashion district.
cards.source_title: St. Andrew’s Church | Monumental Churches of Antwerp

cards.title: The Altarpiece Pulley
cards.subtitle: The church changes monumental paintings with stage machinery.
cards.notes: Behind the high altar, paintings can be released from the frame and exchanged using a pulley system. The theatrical mechanism belongs in this former Jesuit church: its architecture and decoration were conceived as an integrated Baroque spectacle, with Rubens closely involved in the original artistic program.
cards.short_summary: A concealed pulley turns the high altar into a changeable Baroque set.
cards.source_title: Baroque Orchestration: St. Charles Borromeo Church Visitor Guide | Monumental Churches of Antwerp

cards.title: Museum Plantin-Moretus
cards.subtitle: A family printing business became the only museum on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.
cards.notes: The original Plantin-Moretus home and workshop preserves the world’s oldest printing presses, historical type and business archives where the family printed and published for three centuries. It makes sense in Antwerp because the city was one of early modern Europe’s leading printing centers; this is the surviving workplace, not a later collection assembled elsewhere.
cards.short_summary: The Renaissance printing house survives in place, complete with presses, type, home and archives.

cards.title: Nello and Patrasche
cards.subtitle: Antwerp memorializes fictional residents better known across East Asia.
cards.notes: Ouida’s 1872 novel follows an orphan, his dog and a milk route from Hoboken to Antwerp, ending before a Rubens painting in the cathedral. The story became especially popular in Japan and Korea and now has a bronze monument in Hoboken. Its emotional geography only fully resolves here: farm road, city, cathedral and Rubens all belong to the plot.
cards.short_summary: A locally set Victorian tragedy returned to Antwerp as a monument after finding an enormous Asian audience.
cards.source_title: De Hobokense helden: Nello en Patrasche | Antwerpen

cards.title: A Bolleke Keuning
cards.subtitle: Order the glass shape and Antwerp knows which beer you mean.
cards.notes: De Koninck’s amber Spéciale Belge took the nickname “Bolleke” from its rounded glass; in Antwerp dialect, the full order is a “Bolleke Keuning.” Brewed since 1952, it is local shorthand built from glassware, dialect and the brewery’s family name rather than a generic beer style.
cards.short_summary: An Antwerp beer is ordered by the affectionate local name of its spherical glass.
cards.source_title: Bolleke | Antwerp City Brewery De Koninck
